chapter.title: Chapter 32: Keep writing quality high
chapter.body_html:
This chapter covers the following three Skills.

  1. /unslop
  2. /bro
  3. /technical-writing

All three Skills keep the quality of the text the agent writes high. Each one has its own job.

  • /unslop. The agent removes AI habits from its own text, such as stock phrases like "I hope this helps!"
  • /bro. The agent restates its last reply, shorter and without jargon.
  • /technical-writing. The agent first decides the kind of document, such as a tutorial or a reference, and then writes the technical document.

This chapter first looks at how the three Skills differ in what they target, who fixes the text, and what triggers them. Then it explains each Skill from four angles: its role, when to use it, its rules or steps, and how to write the request.

How this chapter is organized

The chapter has the following five sections.

  • The three Skills differ in what they target and who fixes the text
  • /unslop removes AI habits from text with numbered rules
  • /bro restates a hard-to-follow reply without jargon
  • /technical-writing makes the agent decide the kind of document before it writes
  • Summary

The three Skills differ in what they target and who fixes the text

The following table shows what each Skill targets and who fixes the text.

Skill Target Who fixes the text
/unslop Any text, including the agent's replies The agent that wrote the text fixes it by following the rules
/bro The agent's last reply The user calls it when a reply is hard to follow, and the agent restates the reply
/technical-writing Docs, RFCs, READMEs, PR descriptions, and commit messages The agent that wrote the text writes and fixes it by following the standards of four layers

The three run only when called by name

All three SKILL.md files set disable-model-invocation: true (Chapter 25). The agent never picks a Skill with this setting on its own from the content of the conversation. So the three run only when the user calls them by name, or when /poteto-mode, a Playbook, or another Skill names them in its steps.

The "Non-negotiables" section of /poteto-mode (Chapter 8) sets when the agent calls two of these Skills. The agent calls /unslop when it writes any text, and it calls /technical-writing when it writes docs, RFCs, READMEs, PR descriptions, or commit messages.

So when you work in /poteto-mode, the agent calls these two Skills under the "Non-negotiables" rules, even if you never call them by name.

/unslop removes AI habits from text with numbered rules

Role: remove AI habits from text by rule

/unslop is a Skill with which the agent cuts AI habits from its own text by following rules.

AI habits are the phrasings and formatting that often appear in AI-written text and tell the reader that a machine wrote it.

The Skill calls these habits "AI tells" or "AI patterns". Examples are a stock phrase at the end of a reply and heavy use of em dashes.

The rules and their examples all target English text. But most of the rules apply to writing in any language, so they still work for Japanese.

The rules work best in English, so it is fair to say "The hottest programing language is English".

When to use it: apply it to every piece of text, always

The "Non-negotiables" in /poteto-mode require the agent to apply this Skill to all text, including the agent's replies.

The description in SKILL.md also says "Must always apply". But /unslop sets disable-model-invocation: true, so the agent does not call /unslop on its own after reading this description. The Skill applies every time because the "Non-negotiables" rules call /unslop, and so do the steps of the other Skills and Playbooks shown next.

Other Skills and Playbooks that write text also use /unslop

Other Skills and Playbooks also tell the agent, in their steps, to apply /unslop to the text they write. The following table lists each caller and the text it applies /unslop to.

Caller Text that gets /unslop
/technical-writing Every document it writes or reviews
"Opening a PR" and "Multi-phase or multi-PR plan" Playbooks PR titles, PR descriptions, commit bodies, and plan documents
/teach, /show-me-your-work Explanatory replies and the decision log
/recall, /blast-radius Reports handed to the user
/automate-me The draft of the user's personal Skill
"Investigation" Playbook The reply with the findings

The details for each caller follow.

/technical-writing: hands the list of AI habits to /unslop

/technical-writing does not keep its own list of habits such as AI vocabulary and filler. It hands that list to /unslop. So it applies /unslop to every document it writes or reviews.

"Opening a PR" and "Multi-phase or multi-PR plan" Playbooks: apply /unslop after writing with /technical-writing

The "Opening a PR" Playbook (Chapter 14), which opens a PR, tells the agent to write the PR title, the PR description, and the commit bodies with /technical-writing, then apply /unslop.

The "Multi-phase or multi-PR plan" Playbook (Chapter 16) writes a plan document that spans several phases or PRs. This Playbook also tells the agent to write the plan document with /technical-writing, then apply /unslop.

/teach, /show-me-your-work: write the way you would talk to a coworker

/teach (Chapter 22) is a Skill that explains the work in plain words so that a person really understands it. /teach tells the agent to write every reply in plain spoken language, the way you would explain something to a coworker. /teach then applies /unslop to those replies.

/show-me-your-work (Chapter 28) is a Skill that records the agent's decisions and their reasons in a file, one per line. /show-me-your-work tells the agent to write each line of the decision log the way you would tell a teammate what you did, without AI phrasing or abstract jargon. It then applies /unslop to the sentences of the decision log too.

/recall, /blast-radius: write reports handed to the user

/recall (Chapter 22) is a Skill that rebuilds the state of the user's recent work from sources such as the chat history. /blast-radius (Chapter 27) is a Skill that looks, before a release, for what a change might break elsewhere.

Both Skills pass the report they hand to the user through /unslop. The /recall report says how far the work has come and what to do next. The /blast-radius report says what the change might break and what to verify before the merge.

/automate-me: fixes the text of the user's personal Skill with /unslop

/automate-me (Chapter 25) is a Skill that reads the user's working preferences from their recent transcripts and drafts a personal Skill named <user name>-mode for that user. /automate-me applies /unslop to each line of that draft.

"Investigation" Playbook: the reply with the findings is itself the artifact

"Investigation" (Chapter 10) is a Playbook that researches and answers a question without changing code. This Playbook returns a sourced explanation or recommendation instead of a code change. The Playbook defines that reply as the artifact of the investigation.

At the end of its steps, this Playbook applies /unslop to that reply.

Rules: AI habits in seven categories with fixed numbers

The rules take up most of SKILL.md. The Skill has only the following two steps.

  1. Look for the spots that match a rule
  2. Rewrite them, keep the meaning, and match the tone the writer intended

The rules have numbers, and each number is a fixed ID that other Skills use to point at a rule. For example, /poteto-mode points at the rule against using colons as mid-sentence connectors by number, as "unslop rule 14".

SKILL.md says that when the maintainers remove a rule, its number stays empty. In the SKILL.md of pstack version 0.15.5, numbers 1, 2, 4, 6, and 21 are empty.

!

You can confirm the missing numbers in the source view on GitHub.

There are 28 rules in the following seven categories.

Category What it fixes Rule numbers
Content Phrases that only add praise, and claims with no clear source 3, 5
Language Words AI uses often, and fixed patterns of phrasing 7 to 12
Style Use of punctuation, bold, headings, and emojis 13 to 19
Communication artifacts Stock phrases from chat replies, and a fawning tone 20, 22
Filler Words that mean nothing, too much hedging, and empty conclusions 23 to 25
Jargon Metaphor nouns that only sound technical 26
Plain speech Sentences that only describe a feeling, sentences the reader must reread, and fancy words 27 to 33

Next, I list every rule, category by category.

As noted above, the rules and their examples all target English text. Still, in this book, I treat every rule except the four that are specific to English formatting, rules 13, 14, 17, and 19, as applying to Japanese text too. The Japanese edition of this book replaces the examples of those rules with Japanese ones. This edition gives the original English examples for every rule.

Content

No. Rule Fix
3 Superficial -ing phrases Delete phrases such as "highlighting...", "ensuring...", and "reflecting..." that only add praise, or expand them with real sources
5 Vague attributions Stop writing "Experts believe" or "Industry reports suggest", which hide who said it. Name the source or delete the claim

Language

No. Rule Fix
7 AI vocabulary Do not overuse words such as "Additionally", "crucial", "delve", and "pivotal". Replace them with plain words
8 Fancy ways to say "is" Change "serves as", "stands as", and "boasts" to "is" or "has"
9 "Not just X, but Y." Stop using "Not just X, but Y" and state the point directly
10 Rule of three Do not force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number
11 Synonym cycling Do not call one person protagonist, main character, and central figure in one paragraph. Pick one word and repeat it
12 False ranges Do not join things that are not on one scale with "from X to Y". List the topics directly

Style

No. Rule Fix
13 Em dash overuse Do not use em dashes. Use periods or commas. Do not substitute parentheses, en dashes, or hyphens either
14 Colon overuse Use colons only before a list or an example, not as mid-sentence connectors
15 Boldface overuse Do not bold every proper noun or acronym
16 Inline-header lists Turn a list item such as "Performance: Performance improved..." into prose when its bold label repeats the line
17 Title case headings Write headings in sentence case
18 Decorative emojis Remove emojis from headings and bullets
19 Curly quotes Replace curly quotes with straight quotes
!
  • Title Case capitalizes the first letter of every major word in a heading, for example "Pick The Mode First".
  • Sentence case capitalizes only the first word of a heading, as in a sentence, for example "Pick the mode first".

Communication artifacts

No. Rule Fix
20 Chatbot phrases Remove sentences such as "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", and "Certainly!"
22 Sycophantic tone Drop openers such as "Great question! You're absolutely right!" and answer directly

Filler

No. Rule Fix
23 Filler phrases Change "Due to the fact that" to "Because". Delete "It is important to note that"
24 Excessive hedging Change "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" to "may"
25 Generic conclusions Drop endings such as "The future looks bright." and state specific plans or facts

Jargon

No. Rule Fix
26 Abstract metaphor nouns Replace metaphors such as "substrate", "north star", and "flywheel" with concrete words. For example, "substrate" becomes "base"

Plain speech

No. Rule Fix
27 Say what it does, not how it feels Turn phrases that describe how something feels to use, such as "SQL you can read" and "types that follow your schema", into sentences that name a mechanism or a number, such as ".toSQL() returns the exact string sent to the database" and "a column rename fails the build"
28 Shorten or split dense sentences Split a sentence the reader must reread into two, or drop part of it
29 Active voice Change "queries are validated" to "the compiler validates queries"
30 Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb Change "runs quickly" to "is fast" or the real number. For "significantly improves", write the measured delta
31 Prefer the plain word Change "utilize" and "leverage" to "use", and "facilitate" to "help"
32 Mannered prose Replace metaphor and flourish with literal words. For example, "a dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying"
33 Over-compression Rewrite sentences that drop verbs and use arrows or abbreviations as whole sentences. For example, "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing."

How to write the request: call it with the text to fix and extra rules

The bundled guide's docs/guide/05-build-and-clean.md gives the following example, which calls the Skill with the text to fix and an extra rule.

/unslop the readme changes, no emdashes

In this request, "the readme changes" is the text to fix, and "no emdashes" is the extra rule.

The same page says that even with a short request like the following, the agent reads the intent and fixes the text with this Skill.

unslop that, tighten it

"that" points at the text the agent just wrote.

/bro restates a hard-to-follow reply without jargon

Role: restate the last reply without jargon

/bro is a Skill with which the agent restates its last reply without jargon. With a body of only three sentences, /bro is the shortest Skill in pstack.

/bro differs from /unslop in the unit it fixes. /unslop fixes only the spots that match a rule, such as stock phrases. /bro uses no rules and restates the whole last reply in plain words.

Unlike /unslop and /technical-writing, /bro appears in no step of /poteto-mode, a Playbook, or another Skill. So /bro runs only when the user calls it by name.

When to use it: the reply is detailed, but you cannot tell what it says

The user uses this Skill when the agent's reply is technically detailed but the user cannot tell what it says.

Steps: the three sentences of the body are the instruction

The body of /bro is only these three sentences.

Restate your last message. Stop using jargon and speak coherently. State it more simply and concisely, like one human talking to another.

SKILL.md has no steps section, and the agent takes these three sentences as the instruction itself.

How to write the request: "/bro" alone is enough

The bundled guide's 10-recipes-and-pitfalls.md lists only the following single word as the prompt.

/bro

The three sentences of the body are the instruction, so the user does not need to add how to restate the reply.

/technical-writing makes the agent decide the kind of document before it writes

Role: make the agent write technical documents by layered standards

/technical-writing is a Skill that gives the standards the agent follows when it writes technical documents. The Skill splits the standards into four layers, from the kind of the whole document down to how to write one sentence. The goal is writing a tired engineer understands on the first read.

In The Complete Guide to pstack Part 2, poteto explains what led him to build this Skill.

The story started when poteto had the agent write the README for Dune, a framework for desktop apps inside Cursor, without this Skill. According to the guide, the resulting README mixed a tutorial, a how-to, a design explanation, and an API reference into one. The agent also wrote it in fancy prose full of AI habits, so the README was hard to read.

When to use it: when the agent writes or reviews documents

The description in SKILL.md names these occasions: when the agent writes docs, RFCs, READMEs, PR descriptions, or commit messages, and when it reviews them.

But /technical-writing also sets disable-model-invocation: true, so the agent does not call /technical-writing on its own after reading this description. The agent uses the Skill on these occasions because the "Non-negotiables" rules tell the agent to use it when it writes these documents.

Among the Playbooks, "Opening a PR", which opens a PR, tells the agent to write the PR title, the PR description, and the commit bodies with this Skill. "Multi-phase or multi-PR plan", which writes a plan document, also tells the agent to write the plan document with this Skill.

Rules: four layers and the rules outside them

Besides the standards of the four layers, SKILL.md also sets rules that sit outside the layers. I look at the rules outside the layers first, then at the four layers one at a time.

Three rules that take priority over the four layers

Apart from the four layers, the agent follows these three rules, and they take priority over every layer.

  • Cut every word whose removal leaves the meaning of the sentence unchanged. For example, "In order to" becomes "to".
  • Use short, everyday words. For example, write "use", not "utilize".
  • If a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone. The rules exist for the reader. A sentence that follows every rule but reads as if a machine wrote it has failed.

Use the names in the codebase as they are, and do not invent jargon

The agent writes the names of the symbols, files, flags, and commands that exist in the codebase as they are, without rewording them.

The agent also does not invent new jargon. It uses the words a developer says out loud. For example, to say that code moves to another place, it writes "move", not "evacuate".

On the other hand, when an established design or approach already has a widely used name, such as "the Strangler Fig pattern", the agent uses that name.

But the agent adds the meaning where the name first appears in the document. For example, it writes "migrate with the Strangler Fig pattern (an approach that replaces an old system with a new one piece by piece)".

Rule 26 of /unslop, which covers abstract metaphor nouns, lists words like "evacuate" that the agent should replace. When the agent finds a word that is not on that list, it does not edit /unslop itself. Instead, it writes a proposal in its reply, with the diff, to add the missing word and its replacement to the list.

Mix sentence lengths and be specific

This Skill asks for the following four things about sentence length and specificity.

  • Mix sentence lengths on purpose. Use short sentences to land a point, and longer ones to state a fact with its condition or consequence.
  • Decide whether to split a sentence by the number of thoughts, not by its length. "One thought per sentence" does not mean "make every sentence short". Split a sentence that carries two thoughts, but keep a sentence that carries one, even if it is long.
  • In an explanation, give the writer's view. In an explanation, do not stop at listing pros and cons. Also say what the writer makes of them. A reference, on the other hand, holds no views, only facts.
  • Be specific, not vague. Instead of a safe phrase like "schema changes can cause issues", say what happens, as in "a column rename fails the build".

The reason is that a text can follow every standard of the four layers and still read as machine-written if it is all clipped short sentences with nothing specific in it.

Keep a PR description short enough to read in under a minute

The agent keeps a PR description short enough that a reviewer can read it in under a minute. So it links the run logs of /swarm (Chapter 24), lists of commit SHAs, and metric tables instead of pasting them into the body.

The four layers go from the whole document down to one sentence

The four layers are stages that look closer and closer, from the whole document down to the content of one sentence. Each layer owns one question.

Layer Question Key point
Diátaxis What kind of document is this? Make it one of tutorial, how-to, reference, or explanation. Do not mix them. Split them and link them
Google developer style How do the sentences address the reader? Call the reader "you", and write in the present tense and the imperative. Make headings state the point of the section, not only its topic
STE How much does each sentence carry? Put only one thought in a sentence. Use the same word for the same action throughout the document
Global English Can any sentence be read two ways? Write so that the reader never wonders what "it" or "this" points at. Call the same thing by the same name throughout the document
!
  • Diátaxis is an approach that sorts technical documents into four kinds: tutorial, how-to, reference, and explanation. It makes each document one kind, keeps the kinds apart, and links them to each other.
  • Google developer style is the style guide for Google's developer documentation.
  • STE is Simplified Technical English, a standard for English in technical documents that limits the words and sentence forms you may use.
  • Global English is a way of writing English, described in Kohl's The Global English Style Guide, that non-native readers, translators, and agents all read only one way.

Next, I look at each layer in the table one at a time, with the source's examples.

Diátaxis: decide the kind of document first

Diátaxis, the first layer, decides the kind of document first. The reason is that a document that mixes kinds becomes hard to read, like the Dune README from "Role: make the agent write technical documents by layered standards" earlier in this chapter.

Two questions decide the kind: "Is the document for action or for understanding?" and "Is it for learning or for work?"

For learning For work
For action tutorial how-to
For understanding explanation reference

SKILL.md describes the four kinds as follows.

  • tutorial. A document in which a first-time user learns hands-on by building something. It shows the finished result first, and for each step it says what should appear on the screen or in the output.
  • how-to. A set of steps with which a user who already knows the tool solves the problem in front of them. It skips the basics and lists only what to do, in order.
  • reference. A document to look things up in when you need an exact fact. It lists specifications and settings, with no steps and no writer's opinion.
  • explanation. A document for understanding why a mechanism or design is the way it is. It covers design decisions, history, constraints, and alternatives. It is the only kind in which the writer gives opinions.

When a document mixes the four kinds into one, like the Dune README, the agent splits it into four documents and links them to each other.

But the agent does not apply this layer to PR descriptions and commit messages. It applies only the other three layers to them.

!

The other three layers are Google developer style, STE, and Global English. They deal mainly with how to write English. If you write documents in a language other than English, I recommend that you skip the next three sections.

Google developer style: talk to the reader

The agent calls the reader "you" and writes instructions in the imperative, as in "Click Submit."

The agent also puts the condition before the instruction, as in "To delete the document, click Delete." When the condition comes first, the reader can skip instructions that do not apply to them.

For headings, the agent states the point of the section, not only what the section is about.

For example, instead of a heading like "Modes" that shows only the topic, it writes a heading like "Pick the mode first" that tells the reader what to do.
Here, "mode" means a Diátaxis kind of document.

STE: put only one thought in a sentence

The agent writes only one instruction per sentence. Here, an instruction is a sentence that makes the reader do something, such as "Install the component."

The agent also splits long sentences in two. The limit is about 20 English words for an instruction and about 25 for other sentences.

The agent keeps the English articles "the" and "a". For example, "Remove backup file" reads two ways, but "Remove the backup file" reads only one way.

!
  • Why "Remove backup file" reads two ways. The source does not say which two readings it means. In this book, I read them as follows. Without an article, you can read "backup file" as one noun and take the sentence as "delete the backup file". You can also split "backup" from "file", read "file" as a verb meaning "store", and take the sentence as "remove the backup and file it". With "the", "the backup file" is fixed as one noun.

The agent also uses the same word for the same action throughout the document. If it writes "start" in one place, it does not switch to "initiate" in another.

Global English: remove sentences that read two ways

The agent puts "only" and "not" right next to the word they change. Their position changes the meaning. "Only fails on growth" and "fails only on growth" say different things.

The agent also calls one thing by one name everywhere. A document that calls one mechanism "the gate", "the ratchet", and "the budget check" makes the reader think there are three things.

Example: rewriting one paragraph by the rules

SKILL.md includes one rewriting example. Here is the paragraph before the fix.

Configuration of the proto import ratchet budget script parameters is performed via budget.json. Note that it's important to remember that running with --write, which updates the committed budget to reflect the current count, should only be done when lowering it. If exceeded, CI fails.

Here is the paragraph after the fix.

budget.mjs reads the committed budget from budget.json and counts the files that import protos. If the count exceeds the budget, CI fails. Run budget.mjs --write only to lower the budget.

The rewritten paragraph makes the following changes to the original.

  • Drops the noun string "proto import ratchet budget script" and uses the real file names budget.mjs and budget.json
  • Drops the passive "is performed via", makes budget.mjs the subject, and says what it does
  • Cuts empty words such as "Note that it's important to remember that"
  • Drops the metaphor "ratchet". A ratchet is a gear that turns in only one direction, and here it stood for "a limit that can only go down"
  • Turns the passive warning "should only be done" into the imperative instruction "Run budget.mjs --write only to lower the budget."

How to write the request: name the Skill in the request

The bundled guide's docs/guide/09-make-it-yours.md gives the following request example.

/technical-writing review the readme changes

The same page says that the user can use this Skill to review a document that the user or the agent finished. The user can also put the Skill's name at the start of a request for a new document.

Summary

  • How the three differ. With /unslop and /technical-writing, the agent that wrote the text fixes it by rule. With /bro, the agent restates its reply when the user calls it.
  • /unslop. It removes AI habits from every piece of text with 28 rules whose numbers never change.
  • /bro. It restates the last reply, shorter and without jargon.
  • /technical-writing. It first limits each document to one kind, and makes the document something a tired engineer understands on the first read.

The next chapter, Chapter 33, covers /reflect, which looks back on what the work taught and adds those lessons to existing Skills.
